mappings.note: Names an Ayurvedic text finalised in this era. Textual history under the goal.
Names the Hunas as the Central Asian attackers. A name recall; the items that analyse why the empire fell carry LO-124.
Names the Pallavas and their capital. Dynastic and regional recall.
Names ghatikas as the learning centres of the Satavahana and Pallava periods. Educational history; the item on what their founding shows about a dynasty's commitment carries LO-124.
Why the Iron Pillar testifies to ancient metallurgy. Technological history; LO-126 concerns temples, tombs and mosques.
Chandragupta I consolidating through matrimonial alliance and campaigns - strategies for building a state. Not CG-SST2, because the answer is about method rather than chronology.
Samudragupta's mix of conquest, annexation, reinstatement and voluntary submission is a direct account of how he extended control. Squarely the administration-and-military outcome.
What coins reveal about a ruler's appearance, rituals, skills, faith and titles. Explicitly a question about reading a class of source, which is the goal's clause.
Faxian's pilgrimage and its purpose. He matters here as the author of an account of Gupta India, so the sources clause; LO-127 would need a religious movement's emergence analysed.
Faxian's picture of prosperous, well-ordered cities with charitable institutions. Social history from a traveller's account.
The segregation of the chandalas as the darker side of Faxian's account. Social history; the equality outcomes belong to the civics goal and to the present.
Chandragupta II as the ruler linked to the Iron Pillar. A recall of attribution rather than of governance.
The Guptas as the power that rose after the Kushanas. Dynastic succession under the goal.
Names 'Vikramaditya' from its meaning. Treated as a name recall, like the other Vikramaditya item, rather than as an analysis of imperial claim.
Chandragupta I as the grandfather of Chandragupta II. Genealogy under the goal.
Samudragupta as the father praised in the prashasti. Genealogy and source recall.
Harisena as the composer of the Prayaga Prashasti. Identifying who produced a source.
Names 'dharani-bandha' as the aspiration to unify the earth - an imperial claim. Consistent with the other two items on the term.
The veena on Samudragupta's coins. A fact read off a coin, so the sources clause.
Prabhavati Gupta as the daughter who became a regent ruler. Kept with the other regency items under LO-124, since a regency is an arrangement of governance.
Land tax as the empire's main revenue. Fiscal administration, so LO-124 rather than the goal.
Names a region the Guptas traded with. Trade history; no LO covers commerce.
Socotra as a stop on Indian Ocean trade. Trade geography under the goal.
Nalanda as the university the Guptas patronised. Institutional and educational history.
'Classical age' as the label for the period. Period characterisation.
Aryabhata as author of the Aryabhatiya. Scientific and textual recall.
The eclipses and the Earth's rotation as Aryabhata's correct explanations. Scientific history under the goal.
Varahamihira as author of the Brihat Samhita. Scientific and textual recall.
Ujjayini as the learning centre linked to Varahamihira. Educational geography.
Huna invasions plus assertive regional rulers and internal conflict as the causes of Gupta decline. Reasoning about the failure of imperial control, so LO-124.
Who the Pallavas were and where their capital lay. Dynastic recall; the item on their temples carries LO-126.

Pallava Dravidian-style temples and rock-cut caves as their cultural contribution - the style and technology of religious building, which LO-126 names. Ghatikas are mentioned only as a closing clause.
The Varman dynasty in Kamarupa. Dynastic and regional recall.
Reinstating defeated southern and northeastern rulers as tributaries instead of annexing them is a policy of control. The short-answer twin of the MCQ on the same policy.
The Gupta legacy in science, medicine, literature and art for later India. A long-run cultural judgement under the goal.
Indian pottery, Brahmi inscriptions and a stupa on Socotra read as evidence of a sustained trading presence. Archaeological inference, the goal's own clause.

Analyses empire-building strategies (LO-124) and in doing so sets Chandragupta I's marriage diplomacy against Samudragupta's campaigns and tributary settlements (LO-125). Two named rulers are weighed, so the comparison outcome is cited as well.
Weighs the Prayaga Prashasti as a flattering court composition that is still historically useful. Source criticism, the clearest 'how historians study the past' item in the chapter.
Assesses the strengths and blind spots of Faxian's travelogue as evidence. Again source criticism under the goal.
The significance of 'maharajadhiraja' as a claim of supremacy over lesser kings. Imperial authority, so LO-124 rather than a vocabulary recall.
